 Honourable Sri Justice K.Surender

Judgment:

entities.text: Drugs Inspector vs S.Nagireddy And Another
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 1. Questioning the acquittal recorded by II Additional Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Mancherial (for short 'the Magistrate') in C.C.No.395 of 2016 of the respondents herein for the offence under Section 18a(i) r/w 16(1)(a) punishable under Section 27(d) of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, the present appeal is filed.

entities.text: II Additional Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Mancherial
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 2. The Drug Inspector/P.W.1 filed a complaint stating that while he was working as Drug Inspector at Mancherial he inspected Drugs Stores of Area Hospital, Mancherial on 30.04.2013 and picked up sample of drug namely 'Ranitidine 150 mg from the said hospital.

entities.text: Drugs Stores of Area Hospital, Mancherial
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: The Drug Inspector/P.W.1 followed the procedure prescribed for the sampling and accordingly sent for analysis.
At the same time, the Drug Inspector/P.W.1 also collected samples of 'Metronidazole' oral suspension syrup and also sent it for analysis.
During the said proceedings, Exs.P1 and P2 were drafted, which are forms 16 and 17, dated 30.04.2013.
PW.1 received drug analysis report Ex.P3 stating that the drug 'Ranitidine' was not of standard quality.

Accordingly, P.W.1 addressed letter Ex.P5 dated 17.09.2013 to the Medical Superintendent, Government Area Hospital and he received reply vide Ex.P6 informing that the Drug was purchased from M/s.Concord Drugs Limited.

Ex.P10 is the letter addressed to the Managing Director of M/s.Concord Drugs Limited and in reply Ex.P11 was issued informing that the said drugs were manufactured by the 2nd respondent/Accused No.2 i.e.,
M/s.Cortel Laboratories Private Limited.

The Drug Inspector/P.W.1 again addressed a letter Ex.P12 to the Managing Director of 1st respondent/A1 and thereafter, the respondents sent reply along with all the details of the drug under Exs.16 to 25.

Accordingly, P.W.1, the Drug Inspector found that these respondents had manufactured the said tablet 'Ranitidine' which was not found to be of standard identity, purity and strength in accordance with the Indian Pharma Copoeia, for the said reason, the respondents/accused committed an offence under the Cosmetics and Drugs Act, 1940.

3. Upon appearance, the respondents were examined under Section 251 of Cr.P.C, and the substance of allegation under Section 18(a)(i) r/w 16(1)(a) punishable under Section 27 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, was read over to the accused, they pleaded not guilty.
4. The prosecution examined P.W.1, Drug Inspector, P.W.2 was the pharmacist in the Government Area Hospital, Mancherial where the drugs were seized.
5. During the course of evidence, Exs.P1 to P36 were marked.

6. Learned Magistrate acquitted the respondents on the following grounds; i) P.W.1 is not The Drugs Inspector vs S.Nagireddy And Another on 22 June, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64947164/
1 authorized as per Section 22 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act to exercise his powers in Mancherial local limits; ii) The prosecution has not proved that the analysis was done by a government appointed analyst as required under Section 20 of the said Act; iii) any analysis has to be done by a person appointed by the State Government or Central Government; iv) The analysis report has taken several months.

entities.text: Drugs Inspector vs S.Nagireddy And Another on 22 June, 2022 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, as per Rule 45 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, a government analyst has to complete analysis within 60 days failing which, such government analyst shall seek extension of time.
V) The analysis report Ex.P3 was not served on these respondents and by the time complaint was filed, the drug 'Ranitidine' date expired.

7. Learned Assistant Public Prosecutor submits that the sole ground on which the present appeal is filed is that the Government analysis report Ex.P3 is clear that the drug supplied by the respondents was found to be not of standard quality, for which reason, the acquittal has to be reversed and accordingly, the respondents be punished for manufacturing and supplying drugs which are not of standard quality.
8. The record reveals that P.W.1 has not filed any notification to prove his empowerment by the government to carryout any searches or to file a complaint within the jurisdiction of Mancherial.

In the said circumstances, when P.W.1, Drug Inspector has failed to convince the Court that he was, in fact, empowered to file complaint and at the same time carryout search and seizure, the court has no other option but to refuse the claim of the Drug Inspector/P.W.1 that he was competent person to file the complaint.

When the accused has taken a specific defence that unless a person is made a Government Analyst, it cannot be said that any analysis report, Ex.P3 can be relied upon in a prosecution under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.

Section 20 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 reads as follows:
"20. Government Analysts.--

( 1) The State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint such persons as it thinks fit, having the prescribed qualifications, to be Government Analysts for such areas in the State and in respect of such drugs or 2[classes of drugs or such cosmetics or classes of cosmetics] as may be specified in the notifications.

(2) The Central Government may also, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint such persons as it thinks fit, having the prescribed qualifications, to be Government Analysts in respect of such drugs or 2[classes of drugs or such cosmetics or classes of cosmetics] as may be specified in the notification.

(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) or sub- section (2), neither the Central Government nor a State Government shall appoint as a Government Analyst any official not serving under it without the previous consent of the Government under which he is serving.] 3[(4) No person who has any financial interest in the import, manufacture or sale of drugs or cosmetics shall be appointed to be a Government Analyst under sub-section (1) or sub- section (2) of this section.]"

sentences.text: As seen from the provision, the Government Analyst is to be empowered by the State Government or Central Government to discharge his duties as Government Analyst and unless search powers are given to the said person issuing ExP3, Ex.P3 analysis report cannot be looked into for the purpose of adjudication regarding the opinion in the analysis report that the drug is not of standard quality.

10. The learned Magistrate has further found that in the present case, the Government Analyst report Ex.P3 was not communicated to the respondents before the expiry date and the complaint was filed in the month of January, 2014, which is much after the expiry date of the drug.
The said delay in the case was on account of the State Government Analyst taking 22 months for giving the analysis report and the said delay is fatal to the prosecution case.

11. In Medipol Pharmaceutical India Private Limited v. Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education & Research and another in Civil Appeal No.2903 of 2020 arising out of SLP (C )
No.26349 of 2019, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held as follows:
"9) In Laborate Pharmaceuticals India Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (2018) 15 SCC 93,
after referring to Section 25 of the Act, this Court held as follows: "7. The cognizance of the offence(s) alleged in the present case was taken on 4-3-2015 though it appears that the complaint itself was filed on 28-11- 2012.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Laborate Pharmaceuticals India Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (2018) 15 SCC 93
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: According to the appellant the cough syrup had lost shelf life in the month of November 2012 itself.
Even otherwise, it is reasonably certain that on the date when cognizance was taken, the shelf life of the drug in question had expired.
The Magistrate, therefore, could not have sent the sample for reanalysis by the Central Laboratory.

8. All the aforesaid facts would go to show that the valuable right of the appellant to have the sample analysed in the Central Laboratory has been denied by a series of defaults committed by the prosecution; firstly, in not sending to the appellant manufacturer part of the sample as required under Section 23(4)(iii) of the Act; and secondly, on the WWW.LIVELAW.IN 9 part of the Court in taking cognizance of the complaint on 4-3- 2015 though the same was filed on 28-11-2012.

The delay on both counts is not attributable to the appellants and,
therefore, the consequences thereof cannot work adversely to the interest of the appellants.

As the valuable right of the accused for reanalysis vested under the Act appears to have been violated and having regard to the possible shelf life of the drug we are of the view that as on date the prosecution,
if allowed to continue, would be a lame prosecution."

"11) Likewise, under Section 24 of the Insecticides Act, 1968, this Court in State of Haryana v. Unique Farmaid (P) Ltd. (1998) 8 SCC 190 held:
"12.

entities.text: State of Haryana v. Unique Farmaid (P) Ltd. (1998) 8 SCC 190
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It cannot be gainsaid, therefore, that the respondents in these appeals have been deprived of their valuable right to have the sample tested from the Central Insecticides Laboratory under subsection (4) of Section 24 of the Act.

Under subsection (3) of Section 24 report signed by the Insecticide Analyst shall be evidence of the facts stated therein and shall be conclusive evidence against the accused only if the accused do not, within 28 days of the receipt of the report, notify in writing to the Insecticide Inspector or the court before which proceedings are pending that they intend to adduce evidence to controvert the report.

In the present cases the Insecticide Inspector The Drugs Inspector vs S.Nagireddy And Another on 22 June, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64947164/
3 was notified that the accused intended to adduce evidence to controvert the report.

entities.text: Insecticide Inspector The Drugs Inspector vs S.Nagireddy And Another on 22 June, 2022 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: By the time the matter reached the Court, the shelf life of the sample had already expired and no purpose would have been served informing the Court of such an intention.
The report of the Insecticide Analyst was, therefore, not conclusive.

A valuable right had been conferred on the accused to have the sample tested from the Central Insecticides Laboratory and in the circumstances of the case the accused have been deprived of that right, thus, prejudicing them in their defence."

12) Though the aforesaid judgments pertain to criminal prosecutions under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and Insecticides Act, yet, they lay down that a valuable right is granted to a person who is sought to be penalized under these Acts to have a sample tested by the Government Analyst that is found against such person, to be tested by a superior or appellate authority, namely, the Central Drugs Laboratory.

These judgments lay down that if owing to delay which is predominantly attributable to the State or any of its entities, owing to which an article which deteriorates with time is tested as not containing the requisite standard, any prosecution or penalty inflictable by virtue of such sample being tested, cannot then be sustained.

We have seen that on the facts of this case, the sample drawn and analyzed by the Government Analyst was delayed for a considerable period resulting in the sample being drawn towards the end of its shelf life.

Even insofar as the samples sent to the Central Drugs Laboratory, there was a considerable delay which resulted in the sample being sent and tested 8 months beyond the shelf life of the product in this case.

It is thus clear that the valuable right granted by Section 25 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act kicks in on the facts of this case, which would necessarily render any penalty based upon the said analysis of the sample as void. "

12. As seen from the record, Ex.P3 analysis report was not served on the respondents herein whereby the respondents/accused were precluded from challenging analytical report thereby serious prejudice is caused to the respondents/accused.

In the back ground of P.W.1 Drug Inspector (i) failing to prove his authority to file complaint and also inspect and seize the drugs,(ii) non furnishing of analysis report to the respondents/accused are fatal to the prosecution case and for the said two reasons,
the prosecution fails and accordingly, the appeal filed by the State is liable to be dismissed.
Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is dismissed.
As a sequel thereto, miscellaneous applications, if any, shall stand closed.
